name: Data Quality for AI
title: Data Quality for AI
answer: Data quality for AI covers the accuracy, completeness, consistency and timeliness of the rows an AI system reads. Tests written in SQL, lineage records and data contracts are the usual controls, because a model cannot tell a wrong value from a right one. In practice this means checking that values are in range, that keys are unique, that relationships hold and that data arrives when it is expected. The scope stops at the data layer, but it reaches into every feature, prompt and retrieval index that depends on those rows.

sections.body: Data quality for AI covers the accuracy, completeness, consistency and timeliness of the rows an AI system reads. Tests written in SQL, lineage records and data contracts are the usual controls, because a model cannot tell a wrong value from a right one. In practice this means checking that values are in range, that keys are unique, that relationships hold and that data arrives when it is expected. The scope stops at the data layer, but it reaches into every feature, prompt and retrieval index that depends on those rows.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Data quality work runs on the same databases and warehouses that hold the data, with SQL tests executed inside the warehouse or against a copy. Orchestrators schedule those tests, and catalogs and lineage services store the results and the column-level history. This site tracks 2511 active Model Context Protocol servers, and 263 of them are for SQL databases and warehouses, which is where many checks are wired into agent workflows. Metadata stores, version control and CI runners round out the stack, because a test is only useful if it runs on every change.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with profiling: counting rows, measuring null rates, listing distinct values and mapping foreign keys. From there practitioners write SQL assertions for freshness, volume, uniqueness, accepted values and referential integrity, then set thresholds and owners for each check. Data contracts turn those expectations into an agreement between the team that produces a table and the team that consumes it. Lineage records show which upstream column fed a feature or a prompt, so a failure can be traced back to its source. For AI systems, the same discipline extends to label quality, embedding drift and the gap between training and serving data.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance is the record of where each row came from, who changed it and what transformations ran along the way. Rights and risk enter through consent, licensing, purpose limitation and retention rules, especially when personal data feeds a model. A model trained or grounded on bad rows can produce confident wrong answers, and those errors can spread quietly through downstream reports and decisions. Controls include audit trails, access controls, data contracts and clear ownership for every critical table. The aim is to make the quality of the data as visible and reviewable as the quality of the code.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward continuous, column-level monitoring rather than periodic batch checks. Data contracts are moving into code, so schema and quality expectations ship with the pipeline that produces the data. AI agents are beginning to run SQL checks, explain failures and open tickets, which shifts the human role toward setting policy and reviewing exceptions. Quality metrics are also becoming part of the model release process, alongside accuracy and latency. The likely result is that data quality stops being a separate project and becomes a standing property of every AI system.
